newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SUN INT'L DIVES ON LOSS, CASINO PERMIT NEWS.
newsitem.headline: SUN INT'L DIVES ON LOSS, CASINO PERMIT NEWS.

text.p: Shares in Sun International South Africa dived over 11 percent on Thursday amid concerns its bid for a gambling licence in one of the country's provinces had failed and reports of hefty losses at the firm.
By 0912 GMT shares had lost 40 cents or 11.1 percent to a new low of 320 cents in busy trade of over 381,000 shares.
"There is a lot of negative sentiment about the firm," one dealer said.
"Yesterday (Wednesday) there were reports of a 40 million loss at Sun City and it looks like it was unable to pick up one of the gambling licenses in Mpumalanga," the dealer said.

A local newspaper on Wednesday said Sun City, a gaming and hotels subsidiary of Sun International, was expecting losses of more than 40 million rand in 1997 following losses of 39 million in the year to June 1996.
It quoted Buddy Hawton, chairman of Sun International parent Kersaf Ltd , as saying losses were likely to remain significant for some time.
On Wednesday Sun International failed in its bid to get onto Mpumalanga's list of preferred bidders for three gambling complexes in the eastern province.

It named as its choice Tsogo Sun, a joint-venture between a black consortium and South African Breweries hotels unit Southern Sun, and Global Resorts, a consortium consisting of Rand Merchant Bank, Genbel Securities Ltd and Malaysian Mycom Berhad .
Mpumalanga is the first province to give the formal go-ahead for the issue of casino licences following new gambling legislation passed last year.
Under the previous white-ruled government, puritanical laws forbade gaming houses, although gambling was allowed in the former independent black homelands where Sun International resorts flourished.

But under the new laws Sun Interantional will be forced to cut back its operations. No company may hold more than 16 licences countrywide or two in each province -- Sun International holds 17 licences and more than two in both the North-West and Eastern Cape Provinces.
